Specification

https://webmachinelearning.github.io/prompt-api/#enumdef-languagemodelsamplingmode

Explainer

https://github.com/webmachinelearning/prompt-api/blob/main/README.md#sampling-parameters

Links

  • Previous early design review, if any: #1093 (specifically "Interoperable model parameters" in #1093 (comment))
  • An introduction to the feature, aimed at unfamiliar audiences: https://github.com/webmachinelearning/prompt-api/blob/main/README.md#sampling-parameters
  • A description of the problems that end-users were facing before this proposal: webmachinelearning/prompt-api#203 and webmachinelearning/prompt-api#42
  • Alternatives considered:
    • Exposing raw scalar temperature and topK parameters on the open web (excluded per TAG feedback in #1093; deprecated in extension contexts).
    • Synonym-based enum naming ("deterministic" / "precise" / "imaginative") and single-axis naming (AILanguageModelCreativity), replaced after international developer readability discussions in webmachinelearning/prompt-api#203 (comment) and webmachinelearning/prompt-api#203 (comment).
    • Coarser 3-tier or 5-tier preset counts, expanded to 7 presets during the Origin Trial to cover predictable-side granularity gaps while keeping "balanced" aligned with default session behavior (webmachinelearning/prompt-api#203 (comment)).
  • Examples of how to use the proposal to solve the end-users' problems: https://github.com/webmachinelearning/prompt-api/blob/main/README.md#configuration-of-sampling-modes
  • What do the end-users experience with this proposal: End users get more consistent structured extraction and classification on tasks using predictable presets (plus faster, lower-power on-device generation when "most-predictable" enables greedy speculative decoding), and more varied phrasing on open-ended drafting tasks using creative presets. Interactive comparison demo: https://isaacahouma.github.io/prompt-api-sampling-presets/
  • User research you did to validate the problem and/or design, if any: Early Preview Program developer surveys, Origin Trial telemetry, and partner case studies summarized in webmachinelearning/prompt-api#203 (comment)
  • Web Platform Tests: https://wpt.fyi/results/ai/language-model?label=experimental&label=master&aligned (language-model-availability-sampling-mode.tentative.https.window.html and language-model-create-sampling-mode.tentative.https.window.html)

The specification

  • Follows the Web Platform Design Principles.
  • Includes Security and Privacy Considerations sections based on answers to the Security/Privacy Questionnaire.

Where and by whom is the work is being done?

  • GitHub repo: https://github.com/webmachinelearning/prompt-api
  • Primary contacts:
    • Isaac Ahouma (@isaacahouma), Google, feature author
    • Mike Wasserman (@michaelwasserman), Google, Prompt API lead
    • Reilly Grant (@reillyeon), Google, spec editor
    • Kenji Baheux (@KenjiBaheux), Google, product manager
    • Anssi Kostiainen (@anssiko), Intel, WebML CG chair
  • Organization/project driving the specification: Google
  • This work is being funded by: Google
  • Primary standards group developing this feature: W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group
  • Group intended to standardize this work: W3C Machine Learning Working Group
  • Incubation and standards groups that have discussed the design:
    • W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group (resolution in https://www.w3.org/2026/05/28-webmachinelearning-minutes.html#fbac and design thread in webmachinelearning/prompt-api#203)

Feedback so far

  • Multi-stakeholder feedback:
    • Chromium comments: Positive; completed Origin Trial (M148 through M159) and sent Intent to Ship for M160.
    • Mozilla comments: mozilla/standards-positions#1213 (position on the parent Prompt API specification)
    • WebKit comments: WebKit/standards-positions#495 (position on the parent Prompt API specification)
    • Microsoft Edge comments: Positive on interoperable categorical presets even when underlying backends offer coarser granularity (webmachinelearning/prompt-api#203 (comment))
    • Developer comments: Summarized in webmachinelearning/prompt-api#203 (comment) (75% of parameter-tuning Early Preview Program respondents accepted presets, and over 95% of tuned Origin Trial and extension sessions select predictable outputs, with 75% choosing "most-predictable").
  • Major unresolved issues with or opposition to this specification: Mozilla and WebKit hold negative positions on the parent Prompt API specification linked above. Within the parameter-tuning developer cohort, 25% of surveyed developers still express a preference for raw scalar temperature and topK knobs, which were excluded on the open web following TAG guidance in #1093.
  • Status/issue trackers for implementations: https://chromestatus.com/feature/6325545693478912 and https://issues.chromium.org/573612811

You should also know that...

We are requesting a focused delta review of how samplingMode implements the TAG's "Interoperable model parameters" guidance from #1093.

Specifically, the WebIDL surface adds:

enum LanguageModelSamplingMode {
  "most-predictable",
  "predictable",
  "slightly-predictable",
  "balanced",
  "slightly-creative",
  "creative",
  "most-creative"
};

partial dictionary LanguageModelCreateCoreOptions {
  LanguageModelSamplingMode samplingMode;
};

partial interface LanguageModel {
  readonly attribute LanguageModelSamplingMode? samplingMode;
};

Key design choices we would appreciate any TAG thoughts on:

  1. 7 symmetric presets along a predictability-to-creativity spectrum: User agents map each preset to model-appropriate sampling hyperparameters (and backends with fewer distinct configurations may map adjacent tiers to their closest supported behavior without breaking callers).
  2. Defaults, nullability, and legacy coexistence: Omitting options.samplingMode defaults the session to "balanced", and session.clone() preserves samplingMode. While options.samplingMode is non-nullable (so invalid values or null reject with TypeError), the read-only session.samplingMode getter is nullable (LanguageModelSamplingMode?) solely so sessions configured with deprecated extension-only temperature or topK options (without samplingMode) return null. When samplingMode is provided alongside deprecated raw options, samplingMode takes precedence.

Timeline note: We sent our Blink Intent to Ship targeting Chrome M160 on 2026-11-09 (https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/d/msgid/blink-dev/6af20fd7.7772a632.11fdae.052f.GAE%40google.com).

Track conversations at https://tag-github-bot.w3.org/gh/w3ctag/design-reviews/1308

An introduction to the feature, aimed at unfamiliar audiences:

https://www.w3.org/TR/shacl12-ui/#introduction:

RDF applications commonly provide user interfaces that allow users to view and edit RDF resources. SHACL Core, together with vocabularies such as DASH, has often been used for this purpose by describing the structure, constraints, labels, and presentation-relevant metadata associated with RDF data.

SHACL User Interfaces are defined by this specification as a complementary vocabulary and rendering model for generating forms from SHACL shapes. It introduces UI-specific concepts and processing rules for determining widgets, resolving labels, and grouping and ordering the form components used to manage RDF resources.

A description of the problems that end-users were facing before this proposal:

A lack of a formal UI generation specification and dependence on community efforts such as DASH.

Alternatives considered:

Do nothing: just rely on community standards like DASH.

Examples of how to use the proposal to solve the end-users' problems:

SAHCL Shapes Graph defines a data model -> SHACL UI -> a UI spec is generated that can either display data conforming to that data model or a web form spec that can be used to create data according to it.

What do the end-users experience with this proposal:

Algorithms that can turn data specifications into UI specifications.

User research you did to validate the problem and/or design, if any:

Noted the use of community specifications in this area for many years. Both DASH (as above) and also a multitude of non-standardised UI specs, starting right back at JQuery Validator, circa 2010.

items.content_html:
Specification

https://www.w3.org/TR/sparql-rl/

Explainer

https://w3c.github.io/data-shapes/shacl12-overview/#whatsnew

Links

  • The WG's request for this TAG review:
    • https://www.w3.org/2026/10/26-data-shapes-minutes.html#fee4
  • Previous early design review, if any:
    • N/A

An introduction to the feature, aimed at unfamiliar audiences:

This document defines SPARQL-RL, a Datalog-style rules language for RDF.

SPARQL-RL generates new RDF data by evaluating a set of declarative rules against an input RDF graph. Rules are written in a SPARQL-like text syntax.

SPARQL-RL supports negation as failure, which could lead to different inference graphs depending on the order in which rules are evaluated. To avoid this, rules are evaluated using the technique of stratification, which establishes an ordering among rules, ensuring that the same inference graph is always produced.

SPARQL-RL provides grouping and aggregation, with assignment of the aggregation function result to a variable in the body of a rule.

For information about SPARQL-RL in the context of SHACL 1.2, see SHACL 1.2 Overview's What's New in SHACL 1.2 section. In particular:

SHACL 1.2 Inference Rules defines an extension to SHACL for representing inference rules, in particular rules that can be linked to shapes. It was inspired by the SPARQL-based rules introduced by the SHACL Advanced Features and older technologies such as SPIN.

SPARQL 1.2 RL allows the representation and execution of Datalog-based rules using a SPARQL-like syntax. These have a straight-forward mapping to SPARQL CONSTRUCT statements and can be executed within a SHACL Inferencing Rules envelope, allowing for integration with other SHACL features such as node expressions.

A description of the problems that end-users were facing before this proposal:

  • inability to stratify (order) SPARQL inference statements
  • inability to ensure SPARQL inferencing run-once
  • inability to exchange RDF reasoning rules with a standard format
    • since the W3C's Rule Interchange Format (RIF) has not see wide/any adoption

Alternatives considered:

A SHACL-specific rules language which was to be a direct evolution of SHACL-AF. That has been published as SHACL 1.2 Inference Rules but it was still thought necessary, or at least useful, to publish a ruls language for RDF inference without dependence on SHACL.

A mapping to SPARQL is given in this document and, through that, integration with SHACL is achieved too.

  • Examples of how to use the proposal to solve the end-users' problems:

Encode RDF inference rules in stratified and terminating-guaranteed SPARQL-like syntax. These can be stored in .srl files and exchanged. This can replace the various custom rules languages that RDF DB vendors implement.

What do the end-users experience with this proposal:

A new specification for SPARQL rules that can be stratified (ordered, with dependence) and with execution guarantees. This lets reasoning rules be packaged and reused with much more confidence than just SPARQL files which have no ordering or execution guarantees.

User research you did to validate the problem and/or design, if any:

This specification was built on top of the previous Data Shapes WG NOTE output of SHACL Advanced Features. SHACL-AF was never made into a REC in 2017 and yet the SHACL Rules part of it was implemented by vendors and open source communities. We included implementers in this WG to try and improve on SHACL AF and this SPARQL RL specification is one output of improvement, alongside SHACL 1.2 Inference Rules.

We also consulted with SPARQL and SPARQL-like rule implementor communities such as Apache Jena, Python's RDFLib and GraphDB. All were in favor of a tightly specified datalog-style SPARQL-like rules language.

N/A - this is not a browser specification

items.content_html:
Summary

On mobile, subscription video often cannot be played in a browser: the service
serves an app-download page instead of a player, or playback fails where the
browser has to negotiate content protection. Ordinary video plays fine in the
same browser on the same device, so this is not a decoding or bandwidth limit.

Two shapes of the same gap:

  1. The browser exposes a content-protection system the service will not accept,
    so the user never reaches a player. The refusal happens above the web
    platform, and the page has no way to detect it and degrade.
  2. The browser exposes no content-protection system the service can use, so the
    page fails at playback start.

In both cases the web platform has no vocabulary for "premium playback is not
available here": a page cannot distinguish "this content is not licensed for
this platform" from "this browser is not on the list".

The question

Is this an architectural gap that the web platform should close? Specifically:

  • Should there be a defined way for an application to learn that protected
    playback is unavailable (a capability signal), so it can degrade instead of
    failing? Media Capabilities covers decoding, not licensing.
  • Is it architecturally acceptable for a platform to provide its own secure
    media pipeline behind the same API surface as EME, i.e. keeping the sandbox
    while making tamper-resistance a platform property rather than a CDM
    download? If so, who defines the conformance criteria?
  • If neither is acceptable, the alternative is that some content categories are
    permanently outside the web platform on some platforms. Is that an explicit
    design position the TAG is comfortable with?

Viewpoints so far

  • Content providers: the bar is a business/licensing decision above the web
    platform, and it is not published.
  • Browser vendors: the API surface exists; what is missing is a way to surface
    the refusal.
  • A platform vendor willing to offer a secure pipeline cannot express it in the
    current model.

Context

  • Discussion and prior art: w3c/exploration-ig#15
  • Raised at TPAC 2026 Dublin in the Media WG / Media & Entertainment IG
    conversations; a corresponding scoping issue is being filed in Media WG.

Track conversations at https://tag-github-bot.w3.org/gh/w3ctag/design-reviews/1299
items.title: Question: can the web platform express "protected playback unavailable" without breaking the sandbox model?

  • An introduction to the feature, aimed at unfamiliar audiences: https://w3c.github.io/vc-render-method/#introduction
  • A description of the problems that end-users were facing before this proposal: https://w3c.github.io/vc-render-method/#introduction (issuer-controlled visual, audio, and haptic presentation of a credential; today each wallet invents its own display, so the same credential looks different everywhere and issuers cannot convey branding, layout, or accessible alternatives)
  • Alternatives considered: https://w3c.github.io/vc-render-method/#relationship-to-other-technologies (client-determined rendering, credential-type-specific display registries, standalone PDF/SVG/HTML presentation formats, SD-JWT VC type metadata rendering)
  • Examples of how to use the proposal to solve the end-users' problems: https://w3c.github.io/vc-render-method/#data-model (the static, summary, and html render suites, each with examples)
  • What do the end-users experience with this proposal: https://w3c.github.io/vc-render-method/#the-summary-render-suite and https://w3c.github.io/vc-render-method/#the-html-render-suite (a holder sees the issuer's intended card, summary view, or interactive HTML view inside the wallet; a verifier can read a static payload such as an NFC binary payload)
  • User research you did to validate the problem and/or design, if any: Feedback from wallet and issuer deployments during the Credentials Community Group incubation (2023 to 2025) and from VCWG task force participants; specific deployments to be added
  • Test Suite: N/A, will be created when transitioning into CR, following the existing pattern for VC test suites at https://w3c.github.io/vc-data-integrity/implementations/#test-suite-reports, with results added to the VC ecosystem conformance dashboard: https://canivc.com/

The specification

  • Follows the Web Platform Design Principles.
  • Includes Security and Privacy Considerations sections based on answers to the Security/Privacy Questionnaire.
    • NOTE: The VCWG has volunteered to follow the new Threat Modelling approach championed by the Security IG, which largely replaces the traditional Security/Privacy Considerations section with a Threat Model section: https://w3c.github.io/vc-render-method/#threat-model and a more comprehensive Threat Model document: https://w3c.github.io/vc-render-method/threat-model/

Where and by whom is the work is being done?

  • GitHub repo: https://github.com/w3c/vc-render-method/
  • Primary contacts:
    • Dmitri Zagidulin (@dmitrizagidulin), Interop Alliance, Editor
    • Manu Sporny (@msporny), Digital Bazaar, Editor

    • Hendry Poh (@pohhendry), Infocomm Media Development Authority of Singapore, Editor
    • Isaac Koh (@isaackps), Infocomm Media Development Authority of Singapore, Editor
    • Phil Archer (@philarcher), GS1, VCWG Chair
    • Brent Zundel (@brentzundel), Mesur.io, VCWG Chair
    • Ivan Herman (@iherman), W3C, Staff Contact
  • Organization/project driving the specification: VCWG Render Method Task Force; MIT Digital Credentials Consortium, Digital Bazaar, Infocomm Media Development Authority of Singapore, Government Technology Agency of Singapore
  • This work is being funded by: To be added
  • Primary standards group developing this feature: W3C VCWG
  • Incubation and standards groups that have discussed the design:
    • Credentials CG incubation (2023 to 2025): https://github.com/w3c-ccg/vc-render-method (archived on adoption by the VCWG, October 2025)
    • VCWG Render Method Task Force meetings (2025 to present): https://w3c.github.io/vc-wg/minutes/#rem
    • VCWG plenary discussions, including the June 2026 face-to-face: https://w3c.github.io/vc-wg/minutes/2026-06-03-f2f.html#3c9e

Feedback so far

  • Active horizontal reviews: w3c/vc-render-method#66
    • Internationalization (in progress, seven issues filed in October 2026): w3c/i18n-request#325
    • Privacy (closed, no concerns): w3cping/privacy-request#225
    • Security (awaiting review): w3c/security-request#147
    • Accessibility (awaiting review): w3c/a11y-request#176
  • Multi-stakeholder feedback: See "Incubation and standards groups that have discussed the design" above and the task force minutes at https://w3c.github.io/vc-wg/minutes/#rem
  • Major unresolved issues with or opposition to this specification: No formal opposition. Open design questions the WG is actively working on:
    • How a wallet communicates the holder's preferred languages when fetching a linked render payload, which has been raised to the VC Data Model as a general question: w3c/vc-data-model#1653 (see also w3c/vc-render-method#92 and w3c/vc-render-method#89)
    • Linked versus embedded payloads as a general pattern for externally fetched resources, including the tracking and exfiltration considerations in the threat model: w3c/vc-render-method#99
    • How the sandboxed html render suite should handle navigation to and from other credentials: w3c/vc-render-method#99
  • Status/issue trackers for implementations: To be added

You should also know that...

The specification is an extension to the Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.1 via its reserved renderMethod extension point. It defines a single SuiteRenderMethod type that dispatches on a renderSuite value, with three render suites in scope for v1.0: static (an opaque, pre-rendered payload such as an image or an NFC binary payload), summary (a structured, localizable JSON summary the wallet renders natively), and html (an HTML, CSS, and JavaScript payload booted in a sandboxed iframe with the credential supplied as a data block). The html suite is the part most likely to interest the TAG: it runs issuer-supplied code inside the wallet and relies on the sandbox, a restricted set of capabilities, and host-mediated navigation to contain it. The threat model document was written with this in mind.

We are planning to enter Candidate Recommendation as soon as we have received horizontal reviews and responded to requests for changes. This is one of the reviews that is gating our entrance into Candidate Recommendation. Our goal is to enter Candidate Recommendation in Q1 2027.

Specification

https://w3c.github.io/data-shapes/shacl12-inference-rules/

Explainer

https://w3c.github.io/data-shapes/shacl12-inference-rules/#abstract

Links

  • The WG's request for this TAG review: https://www.w3.org/2026/10/26-data-shapes-minutes.html#fee4

  • Previous early design review, if any: N/A

  • An introduction to the feature, aimed at unfamiliar audiences:

SHACL defines an RDF vocabulary to describe shapes - collections of constraints that apply to a set of nodes. Shapes can be associated with nodes using a flexible target mechanism, e.g. for all instances of a class. One focus area of SHACL is data validation. However, the same principles of describing data patterns in shapes can also be exploited for other purposes. SHACL inference rules build on SHACL to form a light-weight RDF vocabulary for the exchange of rules that can be used to derive inferred RDF triples from existing asserted triples.

The SHACL rules feature defined in this document includes a general framework using the properties such as sh:rule and sh:condition, plus an extension mechanism for specific rule types. This document defines two such rule types: SHACL SPARQL rules and triple rules. This document also defines a declarative mechanism for SPARQL rule templates.

  • A description of the problems that end-users were facing before this proposal:

SHACL has long been used for generating new triples, principally via the mechanisms described in 2017's SHACL Advanced Features Working Group Note. This specification improves on, slightly extends and formalises SHACL AF.

  • Alternatives considered:

To do nothing and keep using SHACL AF. This was deemed unacceptable since we have had innovation in the area of additional rule types that can be used with SHACL, e.g. SPARQL RL. We needed to ensure that SHACL reasoning and SPARQL RL etc. were compatible.

  • Examples of how to use the proposal to solve the end-users' problems:
  1. query targetting

Use a SPARQL CONSTRUCT query like this to generate the area of a rectangle:

CONSTRUCT {
	$this ex:area ?area .
}
WHERE {
	$this ex:width ?width .
	$this ex:height ?height .
	BIND (?width * ?height AS ?area) .
}

Wrap that SPARQL query in logic that refines the targetting of only particular rectangles using SHACL.

  1. Rule ordering / once

Wrap a SPARQL CONSTRUCT statement in a sh:SPARQLRule statement that allows it to be run only once by setting sh:runOnce true.

  • What do the end-users experience with this proposal:

An extension to the SPARQL vocabulary allowing for the expression of simple triple-pattern rules, SPARQL rules or other kinds of rules such as SPARQL RL rules.

  • User research you did to validate the problem and/or design, if any:

We formalised the approach taken in SHACL Advanced Features and considered what the inclusion of other forms of rules would require, not just the triple patter and SPARQL rules provided for directly in the document. This was forced by the creation of SPARQL RL but the approach taken will allow other forms of rules too, such as N3.

items.content_html:
Specification

w3c/webauthn#2380

Explainer

https://github.com/w3c/webauthn/blob/main/explainers/cross-device-fallback-url.md

Links

  • Previous early design review, if any: N/A
  • An introduction to the feature, aimed at unfamiliar audiences: During cross-device (hybrid transport) WebAuthn authentication—where a user scans a QR code or connects to a mobile device (authenticator) from a desktop client—the mobile device may not have a matching passkey for the Relying Party (RP). Today, this leads to a dead-end experience on the mobile device, forcing the user to abandon the mobile flow and return to the desktop to try another sign-in method. The crossDeviceFallbackUrl extension allows the RP to specify a same-site HTTPS fallback URL in navigator.credentials.get() options so the remote authenticator device can offer to transition the user directly into an alternative authentication or onboarding flow on that device.
  • A description of the problems that end-users were facing before this proposal: Users scanning a hybrid transport QR code with a phone that lacks the expected passkey hit a dead end on their mobile device with no guided way to recover or sign in on that device.
  • Alternatives considered: Relying solely on client-side timeout/cancellation on the desktop page; or allowing custom URI schemes vs. restricting to HTTPS URLs that are same-site with the RP ID (restricted to same-site HTTPS URLs and checked against CSP to prevent abuse).
  • Examples of how to use the proposal to solve the end-users' problems: Passing extensions: { crossDeviceFallbackUrl: "..." } inside publicKey options to navigator.credentials.get().
  • What do the end-users experience with this proposal: When a user initiates hybrid authentication and their mobile device does not have a matching passkey for the RP, the mobile OS/authenticator UI can offer an option to open the RP-provided fallback URL in the mobile browser (and inform the client that the fallback URL was processed via WebAuthnOperationException).
  • User research you did to validate the problem and/or design, if any: N/A
  • Web Platform Tests: web-platform-tests/wpt#60190

The specification

  • Follows the Web Platform Design Principles.
  • Includes Security and Privacy Considerations sections based on answers to the Security/Privacy Questionnaire.
Security and Privacy Self-Review Questionnaire

Security and Privacy Self-Review Questionnaire

2.1. What information does this feature expose, and for what purposes?

This feature allows a Relying Party (RP) to pass a fallback URL (crossDeviceFallbackUrl) from the client to a remote authenticator over a hybrid transport connection during navigator.credentials.get(). If no matching passkey is available on the remote authenticator and the user explicitly chooses to follow the fallback flow on that device, the authenticator informs the client that the fallback URL was invoked by rejecting the navigator.credentials.get() promise with a WebAuthnOperationException. This benefits the user by preventing a dead-end experience on their mobile device and allowing the desktop client UI to update appropriately once the user transitions to the mobile fallback URL.

  1. What information does your spec expose to the first party that the first party cannot currently easily determine?
    Only two pieces of information:
    • Via PublicKeyCredential.getClientCapabilities(), whether the client supports the extension:crossDeviceFallbackUrl extension.
    • Via WebAuthnOperationException, that the user explicitly interacted with the remote hybrid authenticator and opted to open the RP-provided fallback URL instead of completing a WebAuthn assertion. (Note: if the RP includes a session identifier in the fallback URL, the RP would already learn this as soon as the mobile browser loads the fallback URL).
  2. What information does your spec expose to third parties that third parties cannot currently easily determine?
    None. Cross-origin iframes cannot invoke navigator.credentials.get() unless explicitly delegated via the publickey-credentials-get Permissions Policy, and the crossDeviceFallbackUrl must be same-site with the effective rpId.
  3. What potentially identifying information does your spec expose to the first party that the first party can already access?
    None.
  4. What potentially identifying information does your spec expose to third parties that third parties can already access?
    None.

2.2. Do features in your specification expose the minimum amount of information necessary to implement the intended functionality?

Yes. The extension only sends a single validated HTTPS URL over the hybrid tunnel and only returns a signal (WebAuthnOperationException) when the user actively chooses to invoke the fallback URL on the remote authenticator. It does not expose why no passkey matched, what credentials exist on the remote device, or any hardware/OS details of the remote device.

2.3. Do the features in your specification expose personal information, personally-identifiable information (PII), or information derived from either?

No. No personal information or PII is exposed by this extension.

2.4. How do the features in your specification deal with sensitive information?

The extension itself does not expose sensitive user information. Because an RP might include session context or authentication tokens in the query parameters of crossDeviceFallbackUrl, the URL is only transmitted over an end-to-end encrypted, proximity-verified CTAP hybrid transport tunnel after explicit user action (such as scanning a QR code), and the client enforces Content Security Policy (CSP) checks on the URL to prevent XSS exfiltration.

2.5. Does data exposed by your specification carry related but distinct information that may not be obvious to users?

No.

2.6. Do the features in your specification introduce state that persists across browsing sessions?

No. The extension is stateless and scoped to a single navigator.credentials.get() authentication ceremony.

2.7. Do the features in your specification expose information about the underlying platform to origins?

Only a boolean capability entry (extension:crossDeviceFallbackUrl) in PublicKeyCredential.getClientCapabilities(), which is uniform across all users of a supporting browser version and adds no user-specific fingerprinting entropy.

2.8. Does this specification allow an origin to send data to the underlying platform?

Yes. It allows an origin to pass a URL string (crossDeviceFallbackUrl) to the WebAuthn client, which forwards it over hybrid transport to the remote authenticator to potentially open in the remote device's browser.
To mitigate risks of arbitrary URI scheme abuse (such as javascript:, file:, data:, blob:, or custom app schemes), open redirects, or XSS data exfiltration:

  • The client parses and validates the URL and requires the scheme to be https:.
  • The URL's origin must be same-site with the effective rpId of the request.
  • The client runs Content Security Policy (CSP) checks against the URL so an XSS attacker cannot use crossDeviceFallbackUrl to bypass CSP restrictions.
  • The URL is only forwarded to authenticators over hybrid transport.

2.9. Do features in this specification enable access to device sensors?

No.

2.10. Do features in this specification enable new script execution/loading mechanisms?

No.

2.11. Do features in this specification allow an origin to access other devices?

WebAuthn already supports communicating with a user's remote authenticator via CTAP2.2 hybrid transport with explicit user mediation (scanning a QR code or confirming a notification on a linked device). This extension does not introduce any new device discovery or connection mechanisms; it only piggybacks a validated same-site HTTPS URL onto an existing user-mediated hybrid request.

2.12. Do features in this specification allow an origin some measure of control over a user agent’s native UI?

On the remote authenticator device, if no matching passkey is found, the platform authenticator UI may present an option for the user to open the RP-provided fallback URL in their mobile browser. The native UI remains fully under the control of the platform/authenticator, requires explicit user confirmation before navigating to the URL, and clearly attributes the destination.

2.13. What temporary identifiers do the features in this specification create or expose to the web?

None are created or exposed by the user agent or authenticator. (RPs may include their own short-lived session identifier in the fallback URL query string to correlate the fallback flow).

2.14. How does this specification distinguish between behavior in first-party and third-party contexts?

It inherits WebAuthn's existing third-party restrictions: navigator.credentials.get() in cross-origin iframes is blocked by default unless explicitly enabled via the publickey-credentials-get Permissions Policy, and crossDeviceFallbackUrl must be same-site with the effective rpId.

2.15. How do the features in this specification work in the context of a browser’s Private Browsing or Incognito mode?

It behaves identically in Private Browsing / Incognito mode as in normal mode, persists no state on the client, and does not allow correlating a user's activity across normal and private browsing sessions.

2.16. Does this specification have both "Security Considerations" and "Privacy Considerations" sections?

Yes. PR #2380 adds dedicated Security and Privacy Considerations for the crossDeviceFallbackUrl extension to the WebAuthn specification, detailing URL validation, CSP enforcement, and cross-device phishing/social engineering considerations.

2.17. Do features in your specification enable origins to downgrade default security protections?

No.

2.18. What happens when a document that uses your feature is kept alive in BFCache (instead of getting destroyed) after navigation, and potentially gets reused on future navigations back to the document?

Standard WebAuthn lifetime rules apply: if a document ceases to be fully active (including entering BFCache), any in-flight navigator.credentials.get() request is aborted.

2.19. What happens when a document that uses your feature gets disconnected?

If the document becomes disconnected (no longer fully active), any pending WebAuthn operation is immediately aborted.

2.20. Does your spec define when and how new kinds of errors should be raised?

Yes:

  • Client-side validation errors: If crossDeviceFallbackUrl is not a valid URL, does not use the https: scheme, is not same-site with the effective rpId, or violates the document's CSP, the client rejects the request before contacting any authenticator. Because validation depends only on inputs provided by the page itself, this does not leak any system or user state.
  • Operation exception (WebAuthnOperationException): When the remote authenticator processes the fallback URL in response to explicit user action on the remote device, the client rejects the promise with WebAuthnOperationException. Because this only occurs after explicit user mediation on the remote device, it cannot be used for silent probing.

2.21. Does your feature allow sites to learn about the user’s use of assistive technology?

No.

2.22. What should this questionnaire have asked?

N/A

Where and by whom is the work is being done?

  • GitHub repo: https://github.com/w3c/webauthn
  • Primary contacts:
    • @harshlal028, Google
    • @kreichgauer, Google
    • @timcappalli, Okta
  • Organization/project driving the specification: Google / W3C Web Authentication Working Group
  • This work is being funded by: Google
  • Primary standards group developing this feature: W3C Web Authentication Working Group (in coordination with FIDO Alliance CTAP / Hybrid Working Group)
  • Incubation and standards groups that have discussed the design:
    • W3C Web Authentication WG (w3c/webauthn#2341, w3c/webauthn#2380)
    • FIDO Alliance FIDO2 / CTAP Technical Working Group (fido-alliance/fido-2-specs#1755, fido-alliance/fido-2-specs#1761)

Feedback so far

  • Multi-stakeholder feedback:
    • Chromium comments: Positive; prototyped behind flag (commit 55da8e2).
    • Mozilla comments: Discussed in WebAuthn WG calls and reviewed in PR #2380.
    • WebKit comments: Reviewed in PR #2380 by Apple WebAuthn WG members (@pascoej).
  • Major unresolved issues with or opposition to this specification: None blocking this extension. Future enhancements to bind the fallback URL session to the hybrid tunnel are tracked separately in w3c/webauthn#2478.
  • Status/issue trackers for implementations:
    • Chromium: https://issues.chromium.org/issues/509934168
    • Gecko: WPT sync bug 2042911
    • WebKit: TBD

You should also know that...

The wire protocol and remote authenticator behavior for carrying and handling the fallback URL over hybrid transport are specified in the FIDO CTAP specification (crossDeviceFallbackUrl), while WebAuthn PR #2380 defines the client/authenticator extension inputs, URL validation (HTTPS, same-site with rpId, CSP compliance), and exception handling (WebAuthnOperationException).

Track conversations at https://tag-github-bot.w3.org/gh/w3ctag/design-reviews/1293

This issue was created because the 'horizontal review requested' label was added to

This review is requested prior to the Advisory Committee Review.

New charter proposal, reviewers please take note.

Charter Review

Charter

Diff from the charter template

Expected end of charter refinement phase: unknown

Diff from the previous charter

Chair dashboard

What kind of charter is this?

  • Existing IG recharter

Horizontal Reviews: apply the GitHub label "Horizontal review requested" to request reviews for accessibility (a11y), internationalization (i18n), privacy, security, and TAG. Also add a "card" for this issue to the Strategy Funnel.

Substantive changes

  • The mission, scope, and Success Criteria are retained from the previous charter.
  • The Deliverables now link and describe the current W3C drafts for the Threat Model for the Web and the Threat Modeling Guide.
  • Coordination replaces PING with the Privacy Working Group and updates the relevant collaboration language.
  • Administrative and process language has been aligned with the current charter template.

Communities suggested for outreach

  • Security Interest Group
  • Technical Architecture Group
  • Privacy Working Group
  • Web Application Security Working Group
  • Accessible Platform Architectures Working Group
  • Internationalization Working Group
  • Threat Modeling Community Group
  • Security Web Application Guidelines Community Group

Known or potential areas of concern

Where would charter proponents like to see issues raised?

Please raise charter-refinement comments in this Strategy Funnel issue. Concrete document changes may also be proposed in the w3c/charter-drafts repository, while security-specific technical discussion may use public-security@w3.org.

Anything else we should think about as we review?

Proposed chairs: @jaromil, @patsc, and @innotommy.
